# Writing skills

A skill is a task you have done well once, written down so that the agent does it the same way every time. A prompt is retyped and forgotten; a tested skill can be reused for years and handed to a colleague, which makes it the most durable thing a lecturer produces with an agent.

**Four places to put instructions.** The handbook has now introduced four, and each has its own job.

|  | Instruction file | Prompt | Skill | Subagent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Holds | Facts and rules for every task in the module | A one-off request | The procedure for one recurring task | A role that needs its own context |
| Read | At the start of every session | When typed | When called, or when the task matches its description | When called |
| Example | Notation; "never edit `sources/`" | "Cut the week 5 slides to 20" | A new problem set | The checker; the candidate |
| Chapter | 3 | 4 | This one | 8, 13 |

If it applies to every task, it goes in the instruction file. If you have typed it twice, make it a skill. If it must not see what the main session has seen, make it a subagent.

**When a task is worth a skill.** The task recurs, weekly, annually or across the modules of a programme. There is a right way to do it that you can state, including the checks. And a mistake costs enough that you want the checks applied every time, not only when you remember them. The clearest signal is that you have typed much the same request twice, or corrected the agent in the same way twice. A task done once is not worth a skill, and neither is one where judgement is the whole task, such as setting a mark.

**What a skill contains.** Write it as you would brief a capable teaching assistant who has never seen the module. Template B, the problem-set skill, has each part.

- **Description.** One or two sentences on what the skill does and when to use it. This is the most important line: the agent reads only the descriptions until a skill is needed, and chooses from them. Put the main use first, in the words a colleague would use to ask for it.
- **Inputs.** Which files it needs, where they are, and what to do if one is missing. "Stop and list what is missing" is usually right.
- **Steps.** In order, with the checks from chapter 8 written in as steps rather than left to memory.
- **Output.** Which files, where, and a closing report: what was produced, what was verified and how, and what could not be verified.
- **Prohibitions.** What the agent must not do.
- **Supporting files.** Rubrics, past questions, longer examples and scripts, kept in the skill's folder and read only when the main file points to them. The main file stays short and the detail is there when needed. Template G keeps its examples this way.

Facts about one module, such as its notation, software and file names, belong in the instruction file. A skill that contains them works only in the module it was written for. A skeleton is [template I](templates.qmd#tpl-i).

> **In Claude Code.** A skill is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file, in `.claude/skills/<name>/` inside the module folder, or in `~/.claude/skills/<name>/` for use across all your modules. If both hold a skill with the same name, the personal one is used ([skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills)).
>
> The file opens with a short header of settings. `description` is the only one the documentation recommends. `disable-model-invocation: true` means the skill runs only when you type its name, which suits a skill that edits many files or runs for a long time; template H uses it. `argument-hint` shows what to type after the name, and `allowed-tools` lets the skill use named tools without asking. The documentation advises keeping `SKILL.md` under 500 lines, and descriptions longer than 1,536 characters are cut short in the list the agent reads. Edits to a skill take effect without restarting.

**Put the fixed steps in a script.** Some steps have only one correct outcome: compiling a document, running a notebook from top to bottom, producing the student version of a notebook by removing the solution cells, confirming that each DOI resolves, checking a closed-form result symbolically. Rather than describe these in prose and trust the agent to follow them, put a script in the skill's folder and have the skill run it. This is the rule of chapter 5 applied to procedures: the script does the parts where only one answer is acceptable, and the agent handles the judgement around it. [Template K](templates.qmd#tpl-k) bundles a script that releases a notebook.

> **In Claude Code.** Scripts in the skill's folder are run, not read into the conversation, and `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` in `SKILL.md` stands for that folder's path. `allowed-tools` can let one script run without a permission prompt, for example `Bash(${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/release.py *)`. A line written as `` !`command` `` runs when the skill is called, and its output replaces the line before the agent reads it, which is one way to supply the current date or the list of weeks.

**From a typed request to a shared skill.** Template B did not start as a file. A typical history has four stages.

1. **A request typed three times.** In weeks 3, 5 and 8 the lecturer asks for a problem set, each time in slightly different words. The week 8 request leaves out "take every number from the script output", and one solution contains a number the model typed.
2. **A first skill.** The week 5 request, the best of the three, is saved as a file. Weeks 9 and 10 come out without the omission.
3. **A failure elsewhere.** A colleague runs the skill on a macroeconomics module whose problem sets are derivations. It still asks for generalised method of moments, the Fama-French factors and the week 5 notation, because those were in the request it was saved from, and it has no step that checks a derivation.
4. **A revised skill.** The topic now arrives with the command (`/problem-set week07`), and notation comes from each module's instruction file. Final expressions are verified symbolically or numerically, and the independent re-solve from chapter 5 is handed to the checker subagent ([template D](templates.qmd#tpl-d)). The skill gains test cases and an owner, and is shared.

Stage 4 is [template B](templates.qmd#tpl-b). Set beside the request in stage 1, it shows what a skill adds: the checks are steps that cannot be forgotten, and what is specific to one module is left to that module's instruction file.

**Testing a skill.** A skill produces material students will rely on, so test it as you would the material. Ask two questions: does it start when it should, and not when it should not; and when it runs, does the output pass the checks?

- **Test cases.** Keep three to five inputs, each with a short list of what a correct output must contain, such as "every number in the solutions appears in the script output" or "the report lists the stretch questions". [Template L](templates.qmd#tpl-l) gives the format. Store them in the skill's folder without pointing to them from the main file, so they are not read in normal use.
- **The trigger.** Write five requests a colleague might make for the task and five for neighbouring tasks, and see which ones start the skill. If the wrong ones do, make the description more specific.
- **A comparison without the skill.** Run the same request with and without the skill, each in a fresh session. If the output is no better with it, the skill is not earning its place.
- **Someone else's module.** Run it on a module other than the one it was written for. If it works only on yours, the module-specific parts belong in the instruction file.

Rerun the test cases after every edit and after each update to the tool or the model. A skill that worked in November may not work in March.

**Maintaining a skill.**

- End the file with an owner, the date it was last tested and a short change log.
- When you correct the agent's output in the same way twice, add the correction to the skill as a rule. Chapter 12 applies this to a written style standard; it holds for every skill.
- Archive a skill nobody has used for a year rather than leave it to mislead a successor.
- Keep skills free of student data and assessment content. They are meant to be shared, and anything in them travels with them.

**Skills from other people.** A skill can run scripts on your computer with your permissions. Read a skill and its scripts before you use it, as you would code from a colleague. That includes the skills in a module folder you inherit.

> **In Claude Code.** The documentation warns that a skill can grant itself broad tool access, and advises reviewing the `allowed-tools` of skills in a repository before running Claude Code there ([skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills)).

**By field.**

- **Econometrics and quantitative finance:** releasing a notebook (template K), and generating variants of a question from a file of seeds and parameters (chapter 5).
- **Macroeconomics:** updating data, with official series downloaded by script and the download date recorded. [Template J](templates.qmd#tpl-j) covers the annual update of a whole module.
- **Economic theory:** a derivation check that bundles a script for symbolic verification, so the same check runs on every proof-based problem set.
- **Applied and policy modules:** a citation check that opens each source cited in a case study and finds the claim in it.
